modern_osis:
Leviticus — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)

God established different kinds of offerings and sacrifices to assure his people that their offenses would be forgiven when they brought those offerings with true faith and obedience.

He also appointed the priests and Levites, giving instructions about their clothing, responsibilities, conduct and provision for their needs.

He specified the festivals they must celebrate and when they were to observe them.

Through all these sacrifices and ceremonies, God showed that the wages of sin is death.

He also taught that there can be no forgiveness of sins apart from the blood of Christ, the innocent Lamb of God.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe offerings.1, 2From the herds.3–9From the flocks, and of fowls.10–17
The purpose of the offerings (verses 1–2)

From the fall of humanity until Christ came, offering sacrifices was part of true worship.

Until Israel lived in the wilderness, however, no very detailed regulations seem to have been given for those offerings.

The overall purpose of these laws is clear.

The sacrifices pointed forward to Christ.

They also portrayed the duties, character, privileges and fellowship with God of those who believe in him.

Hardly anything Scripture says about the Lord Jesus is without some connection to his people.

Leviticus begins with the laws of sacrifice.

The oldest form of sacrifice was the burnt offering.

God now gave Moses instructions about it.

These laws took for granted that the people would be willing to bring offerings to the Lord.

Even natural human understanding tells us that people owe honor to their Maker as their Lord.

Sacrifices had been instituted immediately after the fall.

Burnt offerings from the herd (verses 3–9)

When properly understood, the Levitical ordinances used visible things from the natural world to picture spiritual mysteries and events that were yet to come.

Without that understanding, the ceremonies would appear meaningless.

They pointed to the sufferings of the Son of God, who would become a sacrifice for the sins of the world.

A burning animal was only a faint image of the everlasting misery we have deserved.

Our blessed Lord bore the burden of our guilt in both body and soul when he died.

Consider the details.

First, the animal had to be without blemish.

This pointed to the purity and strength of Christ and to the holy lives his people should lead.

Second, its owner had to offer it freely.

Service that pleases God must flow from love.

Christ willingly offered himself for us.

Third, it was offered at the tabernacle entrance.

There stood the bronze altar that sanctified the gift.

The offerer came to the entrance as someone unworthy to go farther in.

In doing so, the sinner acknowledged that communion with God is impossible apart from sacrifice.

Fourth, the offerer laid a hand upon the animal's head.

That action expressed the desire and hope that God would accept the offering as atonement.

Fifth, the animal was killed before the Lord.

The act was to be done reverently, in an orderly way that honored God.

It also signified that Christians must put to death the flesh with its corrupt desires and passions.

Sixth, the priests sprinkled blood upon the altar.

Since life is in the blood, blood made atonement.

This pointed to our consciences being pacified and cleansed when we receive, through faith, the blood of Jesus Christ sprinkled upon them.

Seventh, the animal was cut into pieces and burned upon the altar.

The burning pictured Christ's severe sufferings.

It also pictured the burning love and devotion with which Christians should offer their entire selves—spirit, soul and body—to God.

Eighth, the offering was called a sweet-smelling sacrifice.

God received it with pleasure because it obeyed his command and pointed to Christ.

In the same way, believers' spiritual sacrifices become acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:5).

Burnt offerings from sheep, goats or birds (verses 10–17)

People who could not afford to offer a bull could bring a sheep or a goat.

Those too poor to bring even those animals could offer a turtledove or a pigeon, and God would receive it.

The animals chosen were gentle, mild and harmless.

They pointed to Christ's innocence and meekness, qualities that should also appear in Christians.

A poor person's offering pictured Christ's atonement just as fully as an expensive sacrifice.

It also expressed repentance, faith and devotion to God no less completely.

We have no excuse for refusing the reasonable and joyful service God now requires.

Yet even a broken heart, praise or thanksgiving cannot be offered to God unless he first gives us what we need to offer it.

An Israelite could not bring a bull or goat without first receiving it from God.

The more we do in the Lord's service, the more we owe him for the desire, ability and opportunity to do it.

In many matters, God allows us to decide how much time or wealth we will devote to his service.

But where he has placed much within someone's power, a miserly offering does not express a willing heart and is not acceptable.

Let us devote both body and soul to serving him, whatever he may call us to give, risk, do or endure for his sake.
classic_reading:
[Lev.1.1-Lev.1.2]
Leviticus
God ordained divers kinds of oblations and sacrifices, to assure his people of the forgiveness of their offences, if they offered them in true faith and obedience. Also he appointed the priests and Levites, their apparel, offices, conduct, and portion. He showed what feasts they should observe, and at what times. He declared by these sacrifices and ceremonies, that the reward of sin is death, and that without the blood of Christ, the innocent Lamb of God, there can be no forgiveness of sins.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The offerings. | (1-2) |
From the herds. | (3-9) |
From the flocks, and of fowls. | (10-17) |
Verses 1-2
The offering of sacrifices was an ordinance of true religion, from the fall of man unto the coming of Christ. But till the Israelites were in the wilderness, no very particular regulations seem to have been appointed. The general design of these laws is plain. The sacrifices typified Christ; they also shadowed out the believer's duty, character, privilege, and communion with God. There is scarcely any thing spoken of the Lord Jesus in Scripture which has not also a reference to his people. This book begins with the laws concerning sacrifices; the most ancient were the burnt-offerings, about which God here gives Moses directions. It is taken for granted that the people would be willing to bring offerings to the Lord. The very light of nature directs man, some way or other, to do honour to his Maker, as his Lord. Immediately after the fall, sacrifices were ordained.
[Lev.1.3-Lev.1.9]
Verses 3-9
In the due performance of the Levitical ordinances, the mysteries of the spiritual world are represented by corresponding natural objects; and future events are exhibited in these rites. Without this, the whole will seem unmeaning ceremonies. There is in these things a type of the sufferings of the Son of God, who was to be a sacrifice for the sins of the whole world? The burning body of an animal was but a faint representation of that everlasting misery, which we all have deserved; and which our blessed Lord bore in his body and in his soul, when he died under the load of our iniquities. Observe, 1. The beast to be offered must be without blemish. This signified the strength and purity that were in Christ, and the holy life that should be in his people. 2. The owner must offer it of his own free will. What is done in religion, so as to please God, must be done by love. Christ willingly offered himself for us. 3. It must be offered at the door of the tabernacle, where the brazen altar of burnt-offerings stood, which sanctified the gift: he must offer it at the door, as one unworthy to enter, and acknowledging that a sinner can have no communion with God, but by sacrifice. 4. The offerer must put his hand upon the head of his offering, signifying thereby, his desire and hope that it might be accepted from him, to make atonement for him. 5. The sacrifice was to be killed before the Lord, in an orderly manner, and to honour God. It signified also, that in Christians the flesh must be crucified with its corrupt affections and lust. 6. The priests were to sprinkle the blood upon the altar; for the blood being the life, that was it which made atonement. This signified the pacifying and purifying of our consciences, by the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ upon them by faith. 7. The beast was to be divided into several pieces, and then to be burned upon the altar. The burning of the sacrifice signified the sharp sufferings of Christ, and the devout affections with which, as a holy fire, Christians must offer up themselves, their whole spirit, soul, and body, unto God. 8. This is said to be an offering of a sweet savour. As an act of obedience to a Divine command, and a type of Christ, this was well-pleasing to God; and the spiritual sacrifices of Christians are acceptable to God, through Christ, [1Pet.2.5] 1Pe 2:5.
[Lev.1.10-Lev.1.17]
Verses 10-17
Those who could not offer a bullock, were to bring a sheep or a goat; and those who were not able to do that, were accepted of God, if they brought a turtle-dove, or a pigeon. Those creatures were chosen for sacrifice which were mild, and gentle, and harmless; to show the innocence and meekness that were in Christ, and that should be in Christians. The offering of the poor was as typical of Christ's atonement as the more costly sacrifices, and expressed as fully repentance, faith, and devotedness to God. We have no excuse, if we refuse the pleasant and reasonable service now required. But we can no more offer the sacrifice of a broken heart, or of praise and thanksgiving, than an Israelite could offer a bullock or a goat, except as God hath first given to us. The more we do in the Lord's service, the greater are our obligations to him, for the will, for the ability, and opportunity. In many things God leaves us to fix what shall be spent in his service, whether of our time or our substance; yet where God's providence has put much into a man's power, scanty offerings will not be accepted, for they are not proper expressions of a willing mind. Let us be devoted in body and soul to his service, whatever he may call us to give, venture, do, or suffer for his sake.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe meat-offering of flour.1–11The offering of first-fruits.12–16
The grain offering (verses 1–11)

The offerings of flour, called meat offerings in Henry's English, may picture Christ as presented to God for us and as the Bread of Life for our souls.

But Henry thinks they more directly represent our debt of gratitude for God's providential gifts and the good works that please him.

In older English, meat could mean food of any kind.

Most of this offering was meant to be eaten, not burned.

These grain offerings appear after the burnt offerings.

That order matters.

Without a share in Christ's sacrifice and a heart devoted to God, even our good religious works cannot be accepted.

Leaven represents pride, malice and hypocrisy.

These are the opposites of the humility, love and sincerity that God delights in.

Honey represents sensual pleasure.

Attachment to such pleasure can draw people away from prayer and good works.

Christ's character and sacrifice were entirely free from everything pictured by leaven.

His life of suffering and his agonizing death were the very opposite of worldly self-indulgence.

His people are called to follow him and become like him.

The offering of firstfruits (verses 12–16)

Salt was required with every offering.

By this God taught Israel that even the sacrifices they brought were, in themselves, lacking what made them pleasing.

Every act of religious service must be seasoned with grace.

Christianity is the salt of the earth.

Instructions were also given for presenting firstfruits at harvest.

Someone grateful for God's goodness in providing an abundant crop could bring the first ripe, full heads of grain to him.

Whatever we offer God should be the best of its kind, even if all we have to give is a handful of green ears of grain.

Oil and frankincense were added to the firstfruits.

Wisdom and humility make young believers' hearts and service gentler and sweeter.

Then the first, still-green fruits of their lives become acceptable to the Lord.

God delights in early expressions of faith and devotion, the first ripe fruit of the Spirit.

Holy love toward God is the fire by which all our offerings are made.

The frankincense pictures Christ's mediation and intercession, through which our service becomes acceptable.

Blessed be God that we possess the reality of which all these observances were only shadows.

There is an excellence in Christ himself and in his work as Mediator that no picture or ceremony can fully show.

We must depend on him so completely that we never lose sight of him in anything we do, if we want our service to be accepted by God.
classic_reading:
[Lev.2.1-Lev.2.11]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
The meat-offering of flour.
(1-11)
The offering of first-fruits.
(12-16)
Verses 1-11
Meat-offerings may typify Christ, as presented to God for us, and as being the Bread of life to our souls; but they rather seem to denote our obligation to God for the blessings of providence, and those good works which are acceptable to God. The term "meat" was, and still is, properly given to any kind of provision, and the greater part of this offering was to be eaten for food, not burned. These meat-offerings are mentioned after the burnt-offerings: without an interest in the sacrifice of Christ, and devotedness of heart to God, such services cannot be accepted. Leaven is the emblem of pride, malice, and hypocrisy, and honey of sensual pleasure. The former are directly opposed to the graces of humility, love, and sincerity, which God approves; the latter takes men from the exercises of devotion, and the practice of good works. Christ, in his character and sacrifice, was wholly free from the things denoted by leaven; and his suffering life and agonizing death were the very opposites to worldly pleasure. His people are called to follow, and to be like him.
[Lev.2.12-Lev.2.16]
Verses 12-16
Salt is required in all the offerings. God hereby intimates to them that their sacrifices, in themselves, were unsavoury. All religious services must be seasoned with grace. Christianity is the salt of the earth. Directions are given about offering their first-fruits at harvest. If a man, with a thankful sense of God's goodness in giving him a plentiful crop, was disposed to present an offering to God, let him bring the first ripe and full ears. Whatever was brought to God must be the best in its kind, though it were but green ears of corn. Oil and frankincense must be put upon it. Wisdom and humility soften and sweeten the spirits and services of young people, and their green ears of corn shall be acceptable. God takes delight in the first ripe fruits of the Spirit, and the expressions of early piety and devotion. Holy love to God is the fire by which all our offerings must be made. The frankincense denotes the mediation and intercession of Christ, by which our services are accepted. Blessed be God that we have the substance, of which these observances were but shadows. There is that excellency in Christ, and in his work as Mediator, which no types and shadows can fully represent. And our dependence thereon must be so entire, that we must never lose sight of it in any thing we do, if we would be accepted of God.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe peace-offering of the herd.1–5The peace-offering of the flock.6–17
The fellowship offering from the herd (verses 1–5)

Peace offerings acknowledged God as the giver of everything good.

The offering was divided between the altar, the priest and the person who brought it.

It was called a peace offering because God and his people seemed to share a feast together, as a sign of friendship.

These offerings could be presented as requests for mercy.

When someone was asking God for a blessing, that person might add a peace offering to the prayer.

Christ is our Peace and our Peace Offering.

Only through him can we receive a peaceful answer to our prayers.

But peace offerings could also be given as thanksgiving for mercy already received.

We should continually offer God sacrifices of praise through Christ, our Peace.

Such praise pleases the Lord more than the sacrifice of an ox or bull.

The fellowship offering from the flock (verses 6–17)

The people were forbidden to eat either the fat or the blood of these sacrifices.

The fat meant the fat of the internal organs.

Like the blood, it belonged to God as his portion of each sacrifice.

God would not allow the blood that made atonement to be treated as an ordinary thing (Hebrews 10:29).

Nor will he allow us, even while enjoying the benefits of the atonement, to claim any share of the honor for having accomplished it.

The command taught Israel to distinguish between ordinary things and holy things.

It also kept the people separate from idol worshipers.

The blood poured out and the fat burned in solemn sacrifice were meant to impress upon them the sense that some great spiritual mystery was being shown.

Christ, the Prince of Peace, made peace through the blood of his cross.

Through him, believers are reconciled to God.

Having God's peace in their hearts, they also become eager to pursue peace with all people.

May the Lord multiply grace, mercy and peace to everyone who desires to bear the name of Christian.
classic_reading:
[Lev.3.1-Lev.3.5]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The peace-offering of the herd.
(1-5)
The peace-offering of the flock.
(6-17)
Verses 1-5
The peace-offerings had regard to God as the giver of all good things. These were divided between the altar, the priest, and the owner. They were called peace-offering, because in them God and his people did, as it were, feast together, in token of friendship. The peace-offerings were offered by way of supplication. If a man were in pursuit of any mercy, he would add a peace-offering to his prayer for it. Christ is our Peace, our Peace-offering; for through him alone it is that we can obtain an answer of peace to our prayers. Or, the peace-offering was offered by way of thanksgiving for some mercy received. We must offer to God the sacrifice of praise continually, by Christ our Peace; and then this shall please the Lord better than an ox or bullock.
[Lev.3.6-Lev.3.17]
Verses 6-17
Here is a law that they should eat neither fat nor blood. As for the fat, it means the fat of the inwards, the suet. The blood was forbidden for the same reason; because it was God's part of every sacrifice. God would not permit the blood that made atonement to be used as a common thing, [Heb.10.29] He 10:29; nor will he allow us, though we have the comfort of the atonement made, to claim for ourselves any share in the honour of making it. This taught the Jews to observe distinction between common and sacred things; it kept them separate from idolaters. It would impress them more deeply with the belief of some important mystery in the shedding of the blood and the burning the fat of their solemn sacrifices. Christ, as the Prince of peace, "made peace with the blood of his cross." Through him the believer is reconciled to God; and having the peace of God in his heart, he is disposed to follow peace with all men. May the Lord multiply grace, mercy, and peace, to all who desire to bear the Christian character.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe sin-offering of ignorance for the priest.1–12For the whole congregation.13–21For a ruler.22–26For any of the people.27–35
The high priest's sin offering (verses 1–12)

Burnt offerings, grain offerings and peace offerings were known before the law was given at Sinai.

Through them, the patriarchs already sought atonement for sin.

Now Israel received more detailed instructions for bringing sacrifices to make atonement.

These offerings were shadows of greater blessings yet to come.

Their reality is Christ and the single offering of himself through which he put away sin.

The sins addressed by these offerings were understood to be outward acts.

They were things done that ought not to have been done.

Failure to do our duty is also sin and will come under God's judgment.

Yet something neglected earlier may sometimes still be done later, whereas a wrong act already committed cannot be undone.

These offerings particularly addressed sins committed through ignorance.

The instructions begin with the anointed priest.

This showed that God never established an infallible priest in his earthly church.

Even the high priest could commit sins through ignorance.

Henry therefore condemns claims to act without error as a mark of Antichrist.

The animal was taken outside the camp and burned completely to ashes.

This pictured repentance: putting away sin as something hateful that our souls reject.

The offering was itself called sin.

What was done to the animal is what we must do to our sins.

The body of sin must be destroyed (Romans 6:6).

The apostle also applies the sacrifice's removal outside the camp to Christ (Hebrews 13:11–13).

The whole congregation's sin offering (verses 13–21)

The people's leaders could make mistakes that led the whole community into wrongdoing.

In that case, an offering had to be brought, so that divine anger would not fall upon the congregation.

People on whose behalf a sacrifice was offered laid their hands upon the animal and confessed their sins.

When the sacrifice was for the whole community, the elders performed this action.

The guilt of the people was pictured as a burden placed upon an innocent animal.

Once the offering had been completed, the Lord declared that atonement had been made and the sin would be forgiven.

Whenever churches and nations are saved from destruction, they owe that deliverance to the satisfaction and mediation of Christ.

The ruler's sin offering (verses 22–26)

People who possess authority to call others to account must remember that they themselves are accountable to the Ruler of all rulers.

Even a ruler can sin through ignorance.

That sin must be brought to the ruler's attention, either by conscience or by the correction of friends.

Even the best and greatest people should receive such correction thankfully rather than resentfully.

Each day we should pray, “Teach me what I do not see,” and “Show me where I have gone wrong.”

Then, if ignorance leads us into sin, ignorance will not keep us living in it.

The ordinary person's sin offering (verses 27–35)

The law also provided an offering for anyone among the people.

A person accused of sin may say, “I acted without knowing,” or “Temptation took me by surprise.”

But that plea alone cannot secure acquittal.

The only sufficient plea is that Christ has died.

Even the ordinary person's sins of ignorance required sacrifice.

No one is too important to be under God's justice.

No one is so humble as to be overlooked by it.

Rich and poor meet here as equals.

Both are sinners, and both are welcome to come to Christ.

These laws teach us to hate sin, keep watch against it and greatly value Christ—the true and complete Sin Offering.

His blood cleanses from all sin.

The blood of bulls and goats could never actually take away sin.

When we have the Bible in our hands, our remaining mistakes and ignorance often result from pride, laziness and carelessness.

We therefore need to examine ourselves frequently.

We should study Scripture seriously and pray earnestly for the Holy Spirit's convicting work.

Then we may discover sins we did not recognize, repent of them and obtain forgiveness through Christ's blood.

[Lev.4.1-Lev.4.12]

(1-12)
For the whole congregation. | (13-21) |
For a ruler. | (22-26) |
For any of the people. | (27-35) |
Verses 1-12
Burnt-offerings, meat-offerings, and peace-offerings, had been offered before the giving of the law upon mount Sinai; and in these the patriarchs had respect to sin, to make atonement for it. But the Jews were now put into a way of making atonement for sin, more particularly by sacrifice, as a shadow of good things to come; yet the substance is Christ, and that one offering of himself, by which he put away sin. The sins for which the sin-offerings were appointed are supposed to be open acts. They are supposed to be sins of commission, things which ought not to have been done. Omissions are sins, and must come into judgment: yet what had been omitted at one time, might be done at another; but a sin committed was past recall. They are supposed to be sins committed through ignorance. The law begins with the case of the anointed priest. It is evident that God never had any infallible priest in his church upon earth, when even the high priest was liable to fall into sins of ignorance. All pretensions to act without error are sure marks of Antichrist. The beast was to be carried without the camp, and there burned to ashes. This was a sign of the duty of repentance, which is the putting away sin as a detestable thing, which our soul hates. The sin-offering is called sin. What they did to that, we must do to our sins; the body of sin must be destroyed, [Rom.6.6] Ro 6:6. The apostle applies the carrying this sacrifice without the camp to Christ, [Heb.13.11-Heb.13.13] He 13:11-13.
[Lev.4.13-Lev.4.21]
Verses 13-21
If the leaders of the people, through mistake, caused them to err, an offering must be brought, that wrath might not come upon the whole congregation. When sacrifices were offered, the persons, on whose behalf they were devoted, were to lay their hands on the heads of the victims, and to confess their sins. The elders were to do so, when the sacrifices were offered for the whole congregation. The load of sin was supposed then to be borne by the guiltless animal. When the offering is completed, it is said, atonement is made, and the sin shall be forgiven. The saving of churches and kingdoms from ruin, is owing to the satisfaction and mediation of Christ.
[Lev.4.22-Lev.4.26]
Verses 22-26
Those who have power to call others to account, are themselves accountable to the Ruler of rulers. The sin of the ruler, committed through ignorance, must come to his knowledge, either by the check of his own conscience, or by the reproof of his friends; both which even the best and greatest, not only should submit to, but be thankful for. That which I see not, teach thou me, and, Show me wherein I have erred, are prayers we should put up to God every day; that if, through ignorance, we fall into sin, we may not through ignorance abide in it.
[Lev.4.27-Lev.4.35]
Verses 27-35
Here is the law of the sin-offering for a common person. To be able to plead, when charged with sin, that we did it ignorantly, and through the surprise of temptation, will not bring us off, if we have no interest in that great plea, Christ hath died. The sins of ignorance committed by a common person, needed a sacrifice; the greatest are not above, the meanest are not below Divine justice. None, if offenders, were overlooked. Here rich and poor meet together; they are alike sinners, and welcome to Christ. From all these laws concerning the sin-offerings, we may learn to hate sin, and to watch against it; and to value Christ, the great and true Sin-offering, whose blood cleanses from all sin, which it was not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away. For us to err, with the Bible in our hands, is the effect of pride, sloth, and carelessness. We need to use frequent self-examination, with serious study of the Scriptures, and earnest prayer for the convincing influences of God the Holy Spirit; that we may detect our sins of ignorance, repent, and obtain forgiveness through the blood of Christ.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesConcerning various trespasses.1–13Concerning trespasses against the Lord.14–19
Different kinds of wrongdoing (verses 1–13)

Several offenses are addressed here.

First, a witness sins by concealing the truth when under oath to tell it fully. A person may be afraid of offending a friend or an enemy and therefore say nothing or reveal only part of the facts. But that person bears guilt. Unless something is done to remove it, guilt is a burden that leads to destruction.

Anyone summoned to give evidence should remember this law, speak openly and without deception, and treat an oath before the Lord as sacred.

Second, a person might touch something ceremonially unclean. The contact itself caused ceremonial defilement; but refusing to wash in accordance with God's law showed carelessness or contempt, and brought moral guilt.

When God's Spirit makes us aware of a sin or duty, we should respond promptly, without being ashamed to admit we were mistaken.

Third, a rash oath could bind a person to do something unlawful or impossible. Thoughtfulness and caution before speaking would prevent many such difficulties.

In these cases the sinner was required to confess the particular offense and bring the appointed sacrifice.

The sacrifice was not acceptable without confession and humble prayer for forgiveness.

It is not enough to admit vaguely that we are sinners. Everyone can say that, while remaining reluctant to confess any specific sin. Such vague language can conceal deceit.

Honest, detailed confession is the path toward assurance of pardon and greater watchfulness against future sins.

Even the very poor could bring flour for their sin offering. The cost was deliberately kept low so that poverty would never prevent anyone from seeking forgiveness.

When two birds were offered, one was a sin offering and the other a burnt offering. We must first be reconciled to God before expecting him to accept our services for his glory.

Unlike other grain offerings, the flour offered for sin received neither oil nor frankincense. Its lack of pleasant taste or fragrance was intended to show how hateful sin is.

These sacrifices assured repentant sinners that forgiveness was available, so they need not despair under guilt. They also warned against further sin: atonement was costly and required serious effort.

Wrongdoing involving what belongs to the Lord (verses 14–19)

This section concerns trespasses connected with obligations toward God, including the unintentional misuse of something dedicated to him.

When we suspect that we have wronged God or someone else, we should be ready both to ask forgiveness and to make restitution, even before every detail of our fault is clear to us.

God's law extends very far. Opportunities to sin are numerous, and we are naturally inclined toward wrong. We should therefore stay watchful, consider our steps and pray continually to be kept from sin.

A true Christian acknowledges guilt before God each day and seeks pardon through the blood of Christ.

The gospel offers salvation freely enough for the poorest to receive it, and fully enough for even a heavily burdened conscience to find relief.

Yet the seriousness of sin is also exposed through that salvation. Everyone who has received pardon should learn to hate and fear sin.
classic_reading:
[Lev.5.1-Lev.5.13]
Chapter 5
Chapter Outline
Concerning various trespasses. | (1-13) |
Concerning trespasses against the Lord. | (14-19) |
Verses 1-13
The offences here noticed are, 1. A man's concealing the truth, when he was sworn as a witness to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. If, in such a case, for fear of offending one that has been his friend, or may be his enemy, a man refuses to give evidence, or gives it but in part, he shall bear his iniquity. And that is a heavy burden, which, if some course be not taken to get it removed, will sink a man to hell. Let all that are called at any time to be witnesses, think of this law, and be free and open in their evidence, and take heed of prevaricating. An oath of the Lord is a sacred thing, not to be trifled with. 2. A man's touching any thing that was ceremonially unclean. Though his touching the unclean thing only made him ceremonially defiled, yet neglecting to wash himself according to the law, was either carelessness or contempt, and contracted moral guilt. As soon as God, by his Spirit, convinces our consciences of any sin or duty, we must follow the conviction, as not ashamed to own our former mistake. 3. Rash swearing, that a man will do or not do such a thing. As if the performance of his oath afterward prove unlawful, or what cannot be done. Wisdom and watchfulness beforehand would prevent these difficulties. In these cases the offender must confess his sin, and bring his offering; but the offering was not accepted, unless accompanied with confession and humble prayer for pardon. The confession must be particular; that he hath sinned in that thing. Deceit lies in generals; many will own they have sinned, for that all must own; but their sins in any one particular they are unwilling to allow. The way to be assured of pardon, and armed against sin for the future, is to confess the exact truth. If any were very poor, they might bring some flour, and that should be accepted. Thus the expense of the sin-offering was brought lower than any other, to teach that no man's poverty shall ever bar the way of his pardon. The law of God is so very broad, the occasions of sin in this guilty of. Trespasses against one's neighbor (verses 1–7)

Every offense described here harms another person, but Scripture also calls it a trespass against the Lord.

The person injured may be poor or despised. Even so, wrongdoing against that person dishonors the God who commands us to love our neighbors as ourselves.

Human law may assign different penalties to different offenses. But every dishonest way of harming another person breaks God's law.

Even keeping something we have found is wrong if we are able to identify its owner.

Fraud is commonly accompanied by lies and sometimes by false oaths.

Anyone seeking to escape God's judgment must make full restitution, so far as it is possible, and seek forgiveness through faith in the one Offering that takes away the world's sin.

The offenses named in this law also violate the law of Christ. He insists upon justice and truth no less than the law of nature or the law of Moses.

Keeping the altar fire burning (verses 8–13)

This instruction particularly concerns the daily lamb offered in sacrifice.

The priests were to keep the fire on the altar burning continuously.

The first fire had come from heaven (Leviticus 9:24).

By preserving that same fire, the priests showed that every sacrifice was consumed by a flame originally sent from heaven, a sign of God's acceptance.

Our faith and love, and our habits of prayer and praise, should likewise remain alive continually.

The grain offering for the priests (verses 14–23)

The burnt offering required demanding service from the priests, yet they received no portion of its meat; only the hide belonged to them.

By contrast, most of a grain offering was for the priests' use.

God intends that those who serve him in ministry should receive the support they need.

The sin offering (verses 24–30)

The priests had to wash any garment on which the blood of a sin offering was splashed.

This pointed to the special reverence due to Christ's blood, which must never be treated as something ordinary.

If the meat was cooked in a clay vessel, that vessel had to be broken. A bronze vessel could instead be washed carefully.

These rules showed that the ceremonial sacrifice did not remove every impurity in itself.

But Christ's blood truly cleanses us from all sin.

The instructions also displayed sin's polluting power and pictured guilt passing from the sinner to the sacrifice.

Consider the love of Christ, who willingly became the sin offering for us so that our repeated sins and failures could be forgiven.

He knew no sin, yet was made sin for us—that is, a sin offering (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Through him we receive not only forgiveness, but also power over sin (Romans 8:3).

The guilt offering (verses 1–10)

In the sin offering and guilt offering, the sacrifice was divided between the altar and the priest.

The person bringing it received no portion, unlike the person who brought a fellowship offering.

The sin and guilt offerings expressed repentance and sorrow for wrongdoing. Fasting therefore suited them better than feasting.

Fellowship offerings, on the other hand, expressed communion with God through Christ after reconciliation, the joy and thankfulness of a forgiven sinner, and the privileges of a true believer.

The fellowship offering (verses 11–27)

God allowed more freedom in expressing gratitude for mercy than in acknowledging guilt.

Fellowship offerings could therefore be freely given, making the offerer's willing gift especially pleasing.

Yet God required sacrifices of atonement.

That requirement taught the necessity of the great sacrifice that would reconcile sinners to him.

The chief reason blood was prohibited as food was that God had appointed it for atonement.

This symbolic purpose reached its fulfillment in Christ, who offered himself and shed his blood, bringing the earlier sacrifices to an end.

For that reason, Henry says this prohibition is no longer binding upon believers.

The lifted and waved portions (verses 28–34)

The officiating priest received the breast and the right shoulder.

After the animal was killed, the person making the offering was to present God's portion personally.

Doing so expressed a willing surrender to him.

The offerer raised it with both hands to acknowledge God as Lord of heaven.

Then it was waved from side to side to acknowledge him as Lord of all the earth.

Let us be encouraged to receive and enjoy Christ, our fellowship offering.

This blessed gift is not only for priests or exceptionally mature believers; it is also for ordinary people.

Do not delay in turning to Christ.

Some people plan to repent only when they are dying. But they should receive this fellowship offering now, before the time of God's patience has ended.

The provision that a fellowship offering could not be eaten on the third day underlines the urgency.

It will be too late to seek Christ after death and judgment.

The conclusion of the sacrificial regulations (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.35-Lev.7.38" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 35–38</reference>)

Public acts of worship are not optional matters that we may accept or ignore according to personal preference.

Neglecting them puts us in danger.

Obedience to the laws of Christ cannot be any less necessary than obedience to the laws Moses delivered.

Aaron and his sons are consecrated (verses 1–13)

Aaron's consecration and that of his sons took place only after the tabernacle had been prepared and the rules for sacrifice had been given.

They were washed with water. This signified that they must turn away from every sinful desire and keep themselves pure afterward.

Christ washes in his own blood those whom he makes kings and priests to God (Revelation 1:5–6).

Those who approach God must also be washed with pure water (Hebrews 10:22).

Aaron's anointing foreshadowed Christ's anointing with the Holy Spirit, who was given to him without measure.

Every believer also receives an anointing.

The sacrifices accompanying consecration (verses 14–36)

These ceremonies picture our great High Priest, Jesus Christ.

By his own blood and the power of his Holy Spirit, he was appointed, anointed and set apart for his sacred office.

He sanctifies religious worship so that it benefits his people and honors God the Father.

For Christ's sake the Father accepts our worship, even though sin still mars it.

We can rejoice that Jesus is a merciful and faithful High Priest, full of compassion toward weak and troubled souls.

All true Christians are likewise consecrated as spiritual priests.

We should examine our daily lives carefully. Do we seek to live according to this calling?

Do we offer abundant spiritual sacrifices that are pleasing to God through Christ?

Even when the answer is yes, we have no reason to boast.

We should never despise other sinners. Remembering our own sins and the way God saved us, we should pray and work for their salvation too.

Aaron makes his first offerings (verses 1–21)

All these many sacrifices were brought to an end through the death of Christ.

They teach us that even our best services need to be washed in his blood.

Even our most careful acts of worship carry guilt that can be removed only through an offering purer and greater than ours.

Let us thank God that we have such a High Priest!

The priests were never excused from service for an entire day.

God's spiritual priests likewise have work to do continually, according to each day's responsibilities.

If we want to complete our service joyfully and give a good account of our lives, we must make good use of our time.

The glory of the Lord appeared openly before the people, showing his approval of their work.

We should not now expect this kind of visible manifestation.

Yet God still draws near to those who draw near to him.

He accepts the offerings made in faith.

Because Christian sacrifices are spiritual, the signs of their acceptance are spiritual as well.

When Aaron finished the sacrificial work, he raised his hands and blessed the people.

Aaron could ask God to bless them; God alone could command the blessing.

Fire from the Lord consumes the sacrifice (verses 22–24)

After the service had ended and the blessing had been pronounced, God openly declared his acceptance.

Fire came out from before the Lord and consumed the offering.

The same fire could justly have consumed the guilty people.

Instead it consumed their sacrifice, showing that God accepted the offering as atonement for the sinner.

This pointed toward greater blessings to come.

The Holy Spirit later descended upon the apostles in the form of fire.

The Spirit's holy fire also comes into our hearts, kindling love, reverence and zeal for God, while consuming fleshly desires.

That inward work is a sign of God's gracious acceptance of both our persons and our service.

We cannot offer God anything that did not first come from him.

His grace must provide the holy fire that makes our worship acceptable (Hebrews 12:28).

The people responded with the greatest joy and deepest reverence.

They rejoiced that God had come near, yet bowed humbly before his majesty.

Fear of God is wrong when it drives us away from him. Gracious reverence causes us to bow before him.

These many sacrifices, which were all done away by the death of Christ, teach us that our best services need washing in his blood, and that the guilt of our best sacrifices needs to be done away by one more pure and more noble than they. Let us be thankful that we have such a High Priest. The priests had not a day's respite from service allowed. God's spiritual priests have constant work, which the duty of every day requires; they that would give up their account with joy, must redeem time. The glory of God appeared in the sight of the people, and owned what they had done. We are not now to expect such appearances, but God draws nigh to those who draw nigh to him, and the offerings of faith are acceptable to him; though the sacrifices being spiritual, the tokens of the acceptance are spiritual likewise. When Aaron had done all that was to be done about the sacrifices, he lifted up his hands towards the people, and blessed them. Aaron could but crave a blessing, God alone can command it.
[Lev.9.22-Lev.9.24]
Verses 22-24
When the solemnity was finished, and the blessing pronounced, God testified his acceptance. There came a fire out from before the Lord, and consumed the sacrifice. This fire might justly have fastened upon the people, and have consumed them for their sins; but its consuming the sacrifice signified God's acceptance of it, as an atonement for the sinner. This also was a figure of good things to come. The Spirit descended upon the apostles in fire. And the descent of this holy fire into our souls, to kindle in them pious and devout affections toward God, and such a holy zeal as burns up the flesh and the lusts of it, is a certain token of God's gracious acceptance of our persons and performances. Nothing goes to God, but what comes from him. We must have grace, that holy fire, from the God of grace, else we cannot serve him acceptably, [Heb.12.28] He 12:28. The people were affected with this discovery of God's glory and grace. They received it with the highest joy; triumphing in the assurance given them that they had God nigh unto them. And with the lowest reverence; humbly adoring the majesty of that God, who vouchsafed thus to manifest himself to them. That is a sinful fear of God, which drives us from him; a gracious fear makes us bow before him.

Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire (verses 1–2)

After Moses and Aaron, few men in Israel seemed more likely to receive honor than Nadab and Abihu.

Henry considers it probable that they had become proud and had drunk wine.

While the people bowed down before the Lord in worship, the two men rushed into the tabernacle to burn incense.

They did so at the wrong time, both together rather than one at a time, and used fire that had not come from the altar.

If the offense had been committed unintentionally, they could have brought a sin offering.

But they acted presumptuously, showing contempt for God's majesty and justice.

Such deliberate defiance was to be punished by death.

They died while committing their sin.

This judgment exposed the incompleteness of the Aaronic priesthood from its very beginning.

It could not protect anyone from the fire of God's wrath, except insofar as it foreshadowed the priesthood of Christ.

Aaron responds to the death of his sons (verses 3–7)

The most comforting thoughts in suffering come from God's word.

Aaron had good reason to feel overwhelmed with grief and alarm.

Yet by remaining silent in submission, he showed reverence for God's righteous judgment.

When God corrects us or our families for sin, we should receive his correction and confess that he is the Lord and may do what seems good to him.

Whenever believers worship, they come near to God as spiritual priests.

We should therefore approach every act of worship seriously, remembering the holiness of the One before whom we stand.

God judges people who treat his sacred name carelessly or make light of his worship.

Priests must not drink while ministering (verses 8–11)

Aaron and his sons were forbidden to drink wine or strong drink while they served in the tabernacle.

Ministers of the gospel likewise must not be given to wine (1 Timothy 3:3).

A person may die suddenly, even while drunk.

Since death can overtake us at any time, we should practice sobriety.

Eating the holy offerings (verses 12–20)

Suffering should normally make us more diligent in carrying out our duties, not draw us away from them.

Nevertheless, God makes allowance when a person is genuinely unable to carry out a duty because of a natural, non-sinful weakness.

He desires mercy and not sacrifice.

Let this sad history warn us.

Some people approach worship with great zeal but little understanding, governed by fleshly feelings, superficial thoughts and human inventions.

Their worship may be outwardly impressive, but it is not the inward devotion of soul and spirit.

Their incense is then lit by a fire that did not descend from heaven—a fire the Holy Spirit never kindled in their hearts.

While the people were prostrate before the Lord, adoring his presence and glory, they rushed into the tabernacle to burn incense, though not at the appointed time; both together, instead of one alone, and with fire not taken from the altar. If it had been done through ignorance, they had been allowed to bring a sin-offering. But the soul that doeth presumptuously, and in contempt of God's majesty and justice, that soul shall be cut off. The wages of sin is death. They died in the very act of their sin. The sin and punishment of these priests showed the imperfection of that priesthood from the very beginning, and that it could not shelter any from the fire of God's wrath, otherwise than as it was typical of Christ's priesthood.
[Lev.10.3-Lev.10.7]
Verses 3-7
The most quieting considerations under affliction are fetched from the word of God. What was it that God spake? Though Aaron's heart must have been filled with anguish and dismay, yet with silent submission he revered the justice of the stroke. When God corrects us or ours for sin, it is our duty to accept the punishment, and say, It is the Lord, let him do what seemeth him good. Whenever we worship God, we come nigh unto him, as spiritual priests. This ought to make us very serious in all acts of devotion. It concerns us all, when we come nigh to God, to do every religious exercise, as those who believe that the God with whom we have to do, is a holy God. He will take vengeance on those that profane his sacred name by trifling with him.
[Lev.10.8-Lev.10.11]

Do not drink wine or strong drink. During the time they ministered, the priests were forbidden it. It is required of gospel ministers, that they be not given to wine, [1Tim.3.3] 1Ti 3:3. It is, Lest ye die; die when ye are in drink. The danger of death, to which we are continually exposed, should engage all to be sober.
[Lev.10.12-Lev.10.20]

Afflictions should rather quicken us to our duty, than take us from it. But our unfitness for duty, when it is natural and not sinful, will have great allowances made for it; God will have mercy, and not sacrifice. Let us profit by the solemn warning this history conveys. When professing worshippers come with zeal without knowledge, carnal affections, earthly, light, vain, trifling thoughts, the devices of will-worship, instead of the offering of soul and spirit; then the incense is kindled by a flame which never came down from heaven, which the Spirit of a holy God never sent within their hearts.
